situation:
You are a high-school senior who works weekends at a movie theater, and the paychecks add up to about $640 a month while the summer schedule lasts. A bank teller (judge) at STONEBRIDGE SAVINGS BANK has offered to sit down with you about where that money should go.

You pulled your credit report for the first time last week and found an account you never opened. The same week, a group chat began advertising a cryptocurrency savings offer promising nine percent guaranteed, which asks for your online banking login before it will open the account.

The bank's own savings account pays 0.4 percent and charges $5 a month whenever the balance falls below $300, which your hours after summer could easily cause. An online-only account pays 4.1 percent with no fee, but transfers out take three business days, so the money is not there the day you need it.

Your friends pay you through a mobile payment app that moves money instantly but earns no interest at all. The teller (judge) notes deposit rates have risen because more people are borrowing, and wants you to compare the places and say where you would keep the money. The teller (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are a bank teller (judge) at STONEBRIDGE SAVINGS BANK. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You open accounts for young savers and answer the questions they bring to the counter. You want to hear the places compared on their rates and their fees, hear which one this saver would choose for money that may not keep arriving after summer, and hear what they make of the offer in the group chat.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, how would you know this was the right place for the money?
What would tell you it was time to move it?
